ID: UQ-20261016-22
Date: 2026-10-16
Status: Rejected
Domain(s): Biology — preclinical research methods / laboratory animal science (neighbours: capture-recapture ecology, animal-breeding temperament scoring, trial allocation methodology)
Question (canonical): In laboratory rodent experiments, is the order in which animals are removed from a cage a repeatable individual trait that predicts behavioural and physiological phenotype, such that assigning animals to groups in the order they are caught induces between-group differences comparable in size to the treatment effects such experiments report?
Alternative formulations:
- Is "easy to catch" a phenotype, and does allocating mice to arms in catch order quietly un-randomise preclinical experiments?
- How much of a rodent study's between-group difference is explained by the order animals were lifted out of the cage rather than by the treatment?
- (Gate 1 reformulation, retained) For individually marked cage-mates caught by a standard protocol on >=5 days: (i) ICC of catch rank within cage; (ii) per-rank coefficient for open-field distance, corticosterone, weight slope, glucose AUC with cage as random effect; (iii) does catch-order allocation shift group means by >=0.5x the median standardised published effect on those endpoints?
Motivating gap: Submitted as: randomisation is treated as satisfied once a random sequence is applied to IDs, presupposing that reaching into the cage is itself random, a step said to be unreported and outside ARRIVE's scope. Gate 2 falsified the qualitative premise: ARRIVE 2.0's Item 4 Explanation and Elaboration states that selecting an animal "at random (i.e., haphazardly or arbitrarily) from a cage is not statistically random", names researcher judgement as the bias and allocation concealment as the remedy. What is missing is quantification, not the question. Full record: batches/2026-10-16-0833/UQ-20261016-22-record.md
Presuppositions:
1. Catch order is recordable without perturbing phenotype — low risk (marking + log).
2. LOAD-BEARING AND CONTESTED: catch rank has non-zero within-individual repeatability. Nearest evidence is negative — Jolly et al. 2019 (BES 73:129): repeatable boldness, no detectable between-individual variation in detection probability. If ICC ~ 0 the question collapses.
3. CONTESTED: catch-order allocation is common practice — undocumented; ARRIVE warns against it (weaker than evidence); careful labs already randomise within-cage order (Varholick et al. 2019).
4. Endpoints carry exploitable between-individual variance — partly supported (within-cage R^2 0.01-0.17), but null for faecal glucocorticoid metabolites and EPM.
5. Order effects reflect a stable trait, not transient cohort-removal stress — a transient channel is independently documented.
6. Not presupposed: that the effect is large (criterion is comparative).
What would count as an answer: Pre-registered three-part study — (i) ICC with CI for catch rank over >=5 days, cage and day random effects, rank analysed ordinally and as first-vs-last; (ii) endpoint regressions on catch rank with a design arm separating stable trait from removal-order stress; (iii) simulation over fitted coefficients, or a direct catch-ordered vs catch-randomised allocation contrast, against a pre-specified published effect-size distribution. "Yes" = ICC lower bound > 0 AND criterion (iii) met; "no" = a >=90%-powered null on (i) or (iii). A practice survey is not an answer.
Novelty — queries run (query → one-line result): 11 web searches (search cap reached), 6 fetches, 5 successful; full list in batches/2026-10-16-0833/UQ-20261016-22-record.md. Most informative: (1) mandatory own-field own-words title "order of capture from the cage predicts behaviour and corticosterone in mice" → no lab-rodent hit on catch order, only cage-change/housing-stress and a lizard capture-corticosterone paper; (2) "order of capture" mice cage selection bias randomisation → guideline pages only (ARRIVE Item 4, NC3Rs), first sign the topic lives in guidance not data; (3) NC3Rs "picking animals" out of the cage "is not random" → same guideline cluster, hazard taught but not measured; (4) "catch order" repeatability boldness trappability rodents → ecology hits incl. "Bias averted: personality may not influence trappability"; (7) catch order predicts phenotype laboratory mice allocation → Varholick et al. 2019 within-cage dominance variation; (9) answer-side: non-randomised animal studies overestimate effect size → Hirst et al. 2014 aggregate evidence, catch-order channel absent; (11) fraction-of-X limb: share of papers reporting how animals were selected from the cage → reporting-quality corpora exist, no published figure for the narrower quantity, none asserted. Decisive fetch: EQUATOR ARRIVE Item 4 E&E page (quote above).
Novelty — nearest prior formulations (3, with sources):
1. ARRIVE 2.0 E&E, Item 4 Randomisation (Percie du Sert et al. 2020, PLoS Biology; resources.equator-network.org/reporting-guidelines/arrive/items/randomisation.html, opened 2026-10-16) — haphazard selection from a cage is not statistically random; selection bias; allocation concealment prescribed.
2. Schipper et al. 2025, Physiol Behav 293:114859, doi:10.1016/j.physbeh.2025.114859 (abstract via Refinement Database; full text not opened) — within-cage testing order and hierarchical status affect open-field, EPM and three-chamber outcomes.
3. Varholick et al. 2019, Sci Rep 9:13650, doi:10.1038/s41598-019-49612-0 (full text opened) — dominance rank explains R^2 0.02-0.11 / 0.01-0.17 of within-cage phenotypic variation; no association for faecal glucocorticoid metabolites; within-cage order randomised and counterbalanced as standard practice.
Not verified in Gate 2 and not relied on: Hurst & West 2010; Biro & Dingemanse 2009; Hirst et al. 2014; Front Behav Neurosci 2016 10:99; Wildlife Research WR20121 (fetch blocked).
Novelty — how this differs from each: vs 1 — the guideline poses the hazard and stops, gives no ICC, no endpoint regression, no magnitude comparison, and locates the bias in experimenter judgement rather than in a repeatable animal trait; the candidate's distinct content is the trait framing plus three unmeasured quantities, i.e. a quantification of an asked question, not a new question. vs 2 — same endpoint family and an order variable that already moves those endpoints, but order is experimenter-assigned testing sequence, not catch rank; no cross-day repeatability, no effect-size benchmark. vs 3 — same target quantity (exploitable within-cage variance) via a different measured trait, and it shows the candidate's proposed fix is already standard in careful labs. vs Jolly 2019 — directly tests the load-bearing presupposition in a neighbouring field and finds against it; the lab regime differs (seconds of hand capture vs baited trapping), so the null is not entailed, but the nearest evidence points the wrong way.
Novelty confidence: Low — and lower than the record argued, on the judge's post-Gate-5 verification (2026-10-16, independent fresh-context sweep, 21 queries, 0 refusals). The first half of the record's reasoning is CONFIRMED: the hazard is on the record in the candidate's own field. ARRIVE 2.0 Item 4a states that selecting an animal "at random (i.e., haphazardly or arbitrarily)" from a cage is not statistically random, names researcher judgement as the mechanism and prescribes allocation concealment, citing no measurement; NC3Rs guidance names the easier-to-catch mechanism in so many words. The second half — that the magnitude has never been measured — is REFUTED, and this is a correction to the entry, not a flourish. **Takao et al. 2016, Front Behav Neurosci 10:99** measured removal-order effects on rectal temperature, hot-plate latency, elevated-plus-maze open-arm time and plasma corticosterone in roughly 1,700 control C57BL/6J mice, nine years before the record's headline prior. Schipper et al. 2025 is therefore neither the first nor the strongest measurement and must not be cited as if it were; its Methods could not be read, so whether its "testing order" is physical catch order or a pre-assigned order is unverified. What survives as genuinely unmeasured is narrower and is the only thing a successor should claim: (i) no study measures the **repeatability** of catch order as a stable individual trait across days (ICC or equivalent) — the only repeatability work is on wild-rodent trappability, a different construct, and it concluded trappability is not a personality proxy; and (ii) no study benchmarks an order-induced shift in group means against **published treatment effect sizes**. Restated as those two gaps the claim is confirmed; as the record wrote it, it is not.
Significance — consequence: If yes, the physical selection step becomes a reportable item with a free fix (catch all, then allocate) and an aggregate bias gains an identified, checkable mechanism. If no, a worry currently resting in guidance without evidence is retired and checklist length is spared. A null on (i) with a positive (ii) would relocate the effect to transient cohort-removal stress, fixed by holding time rather than allocation.
Significance — audience: Guideline and funder bodies (ARRIVE/NC3Rs, EQUATOR, journal checklists) who already assert the hazard; facility managers writing catch-then-allocate SOPs at near-zero cost; behavioural and metabolic phenotyping labs; SYRCLE risk-of-bias assessors judging what "randomised" is worth. Conceded weakness: a "yes" mainly adds compliance pressure for an action already prescribed.
Significance — fecundity: Opens strain-dependence of catch rank (a confound in strain comparisons), catch rank as a cheap dominance proxy, catch rank and attrition as informative censoring, the same logic in larger animals, and a general audit of the uncontrolled physical steps between a randomisation list and the bench.
Significance — anchoring: Preclinical reproducibility and the non-randomisation/effect-inflation finding (Hirst et al. 2014, unopened); contested individual heterogeneity in detection probability in capture-recapture ecology; allocation-concealment subversion in clinical trials; the within-cage phenotypic-variation literature that supplies the variance budget.
Reason for silence: Not "no one thought of it" — it is in print in ARRIVE's own E&E. Credible mechanism: guideline-closure incentive gap (once a guideline asserts a bias and prescribes a free remedy, measuring its magnitude is unrewarding and mildly unwelcome either way), compounded by a disciplinary boundary (capture heterogeneity is measured rigorously by behavioural ecologists with no stake in lab allocation) and a documentation boundary (catch order is tacit and absent from methods sections, so it is only studiable prospectively).
Adversarial log (8 rows: attack | objection | response | status):
1 Triviality | not run | — | Not run (candidate failed at Gate 2; no adversary spawned)
2 Disguise | not run | — | NOT EXECUTED — Disguise is unverified; per the adversary-independence rule this entry could not have been Validated regardless of the Gate 2 outcome
3 Combinatorial novelty | not run | — | Not run
4 Presupposition failure | not run | — | Not run (Gate 2 itself surfaced a direct negative on presupposition 2 and falsified the motivating premise)
5 Vagueness | not run | — | Not run
6 Significance inflation | not run | — | Not run
7 Reason for silence | not run | — | Not run
8 Dissolution | not run | — | Not run
Scores: Well-posedness 3/3 · Significance 2/3
Strongest remaining objection: The question is a known one with a partly published answer. ARRIVE 2.0's randomisation E&E poses the concern in the field's own words and prescribes the remedy, and the magnitude has already been measured once at scale — Takao et al. 2016 (Front Behav Neurosci 10:99) on ~1,700 control C57BL/6J mice, across rectal temperature, hot-plate latency, elevated-plus-maze open-arm time and plasma corticosterone — with Schipper et al. 2025 adding within-cage order effects on three behavioural tests. A candidate whose novelty rests on "never measured" is therefore mis-specified at Gate 2, and the residue is two specific quantities (catch-rank repeatability as a trait; the group-mean shift benchmarked against published effect sizes) rather than the question as posed.
Suggested first step toward an answer (pointer only — do not take it): Not pursued here. As an open problem it begins by reading Takao et al. 2016 in full to fix exactly which endpoints and which order construct it covered, because that decides what is left; only then a single-lab repeatability log of catch rank in individually marked cage-mates across at least five days, reporting an ICC, followed by the group-mean shift benchmarked against published effect sizes for the same endpoints.
Routing (if rejected as already-asked): Asked-but-still-open for the two residuals only, and routed on that narrowed basis. The hazard is asserted and prescribed against in print without measurement (ARRIVE 2.0 Item 4a, https://resources.equator-network.org/reporting-guidelines/arrive/items/randomisation.html), while the endpoint-effect half of the magnitude question is already partly answered (Takao et al. 2016, Front Behav Neurosci 10:99) — so the routed problem is the repeatability-as-trait limb and the benchmark-against-treatment-effects limb, not a re-run of Takao. The row in ledger/routed-open-problems.md is written that way deliberately, so the research run does not redo published work.

ID: UQ-20261016-23
Date: 2026-10-16
Status: Provisional
Domain(s): Medicine — clinical pharmacology / lactation pharmacotherapy; method transplanted from veterinary pharmacology and food-residue regulation (EMA CVMP / FDA CVM withdrawal-period determination)
Question (canonical): For a pre-specified list of the drugs most often prescribed to lactating women, (A) what fraction have published human milk concentration-time data satisfying each design criterion a veterinary regulator imposes on a milk residue-depletion study (milked-subject count, number and spacing of post-dose time points, terminal-phase coverage, assay LOQ relative to the limit, licensed-regimen dosing); and (B) for the qualifying subset, what breastfeeding-interruption intervals follow when the veterinary tolerance-limit rule (upper one-sided 95/95) is applied against each of a pre-stated set of candidate infant-exposure limits, and how does that distribution compare, drug by drug, with the interruption advice mothers are given now?
Alternative formulations:
- Could the procedure food-animal regulators use to set milk withdrawal times be applied to human breastfeeding advice, and for how many drugs do existing data already allow the calculation?
- Is "pump and dump" advice reconstructible as a quantitative withdrawal period, or do human lactation data fail a standard the same calculation meets in dairy cattle?
- (Gate 0 intake version, with a single stated infant-exposure limit, reformulated once at Gate 1; both recorded in batches/2026-10-16-0833/UQ-20261016-23-record.md.)
Motivating gap: Veterinary regulation settles a structurally identical decision — how long after dosing milk is unfit for a consumer — with a specified study design, a statutory residue limit and an auditable tolerance-limit rule (EMA CVMP adopted milk-withdrawal guideline rev 1; RIVM MILKINGS calculator), and has even reasoned about children's milk intake (EMA CVMP position paper on MRLs in milk considering daily intake of children). Human lactation advice for the same decision is given in round hours from relative-infant-dose rules of thumb and consensus, with a computed-interval precedent only in radiopharmaceuticals.
Presuppositions: (1) the veterinary between-subject tolerance-limit statistic transfers to milk-volume/fat/schedule variation — graded PLAUSIBLE in the record, re-graded CONTESTED at Gate 4 (the veterinary statistic bounds per-subject crossing times and concentrations; every candidate human limit is a dose, so a volume/bioavailability conversion must be stated); (2) CONTESTED AND CENTRAL: an MRL-analogous infant-exposure limit can be defined — none is agreed, handled by pre-stating a set; (3) CONTESTED: milk concentration-time data are extractable at the required resolution; (4) CONTESTED: milk concentration is the right endpoint rather than infant systemic exposure after oral bioavailability — now contested by three independent groups (concePTION/Milk4baby, Utrecht PBPK, Waterloo UAR); (5) the drug list is enumerable despite poor coding of lactation status; (6) NOT presupposed that current advice is wrong.
What would count as an answer: a pre-registered extraction over a named drug list and named sources reporting per drug, per criterion, pass/fail against criteria fixed in advance from the EMA CVMP milk-withdrawal guideline; then, for qualifiers, intervals computed under the tolerance-limit rule against each pre-stated limit, tabulated beside current advice with a signed discrepancy distribution and sensitivity over limits. A near-zero census would be a complete answer, naming the missing study design in regulator-legible units. Not an answer: advocacy of the transplant, or a framework/decision tree without the census and the computation.
Novelty — queries run (query → one-line result): 40 distinct queries — 13 at Gate 2 (full list and one-line results in batches/2026-10-16-0833/UQ-20261016-23-record.md) and 27 across three adversaries in new vocabularies (UQ-20261016-23-adversary-1/-2/-3.md). Most informative: "veterinary milk withdrawal period method applied to human breastfeeding maximum residue limit infant exposure analogy" → veterinary documents only, no human application; "'tolerance limit' OR '95/95' … applied to human lactation drug milk residue depletion curve" → exclusively veterinary; German "Wartezeit/Karenzzeit … Muttermilch" and Japanese/French/Spanish equivalents (A1 q4, A2 q1, A3 q2, A3 q6) → the veterinary withdrawal vocabulary is absent from human lactation literature in five languages; "proportion of medications lacking human lactation pharmacokinetic data analysis of LactMed records percentage measured milk concentrations" (A3 q4) → Fomina 2023, the published census the record said it could not obtain; "appraisal of human milk pharmacokinetic studies against FDA lactation guidance … sampling adequacy systematic review" (A3 q7) → Meer 2015, limb A already executed for one drug class against an external design standard; "systematic review completeness reporting human milk pharmacokinetic studies percentage reported number of subjects sampling duration assay LOQ" (A1 q6) → Manitoba "Medications in human milk" thesis, 224 studies / 186 medications; "human milk bank donor medication deferral period … guidelines" (A3 q1) → FSANZ 2019 imported-food advice recording a 5 × half-life donor deferral rule.
Novelty — nearest prior formulations (3, with sources):
1. Fomina YY, Byrne JJ, Spong CY. "Evaluating strength of recommendations for commonly administered medications in lactating women." J Matern Fetal Neonatal Med 2023;36(1):2163626, DOI 10.1080/14767058.2022.2163626. Opened and quoted by adversary 3: all 1408 LactMed medications plus "the most commonly used medications in lactating women as defined by prior literature"; "714 (51%) had no associated data, 664 (47%) had minimal-moderate data, and 30 (2%) had strong data", strong = studies in all four LactMed categories including maternal and infant drug levels. DOI/venue independently located by adversary 2; the 1408/2% figure independently corroborated from Yeung CHT et al., Front Pediatr 2023;11:1147566 (opened by adversary 2).
2. Meer DH, Wieringa A, Wegner I, Wilffert B, ter Horst PGJ. "Lactation studies of anticonvulsants: a quality review." Br J Clin Pharmacol 2015;79(4):558–565, DOI 10.1111/bcp.12524. Opened and quoted by adversary 3: 62 studies, 19 anticonvulsants, audited "against the guidelines of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)" and ILCA, faulting "the number of samples in a particular dose interval" and "the low number of study participants"; 25/62 were case reports, letters or abstracts.
3. Damoiseaux D et al. "Predicting Chemotherapy Distribution into Breast Milk for Breastfeeding Women Using a Population Pharmacokinetic Approach." Clin Pharmacokinet 2023;62(7):969–980 (PMC10338611), opened by adversary 1: discard days for 3 cytotoxics against a pre-stated set of candidate limits — 1%, 0.1%, 0.01% cumulative RID, "chosen for demonstration purposes" — read off upper prediction limits. Companion PBPK paper CPT:PSP 2023;12(12):1931–1944, DOI 10.1002/psp4.13043 (2 drugs, pre-set 3-day discard, no stated threshold) opened by adversaries 1 and 2.
Further neighbours: Monfort A et al., Front Pharmacol 2025;16:1602018 (Milk4baby decision tree, 50 medications; opened at Gate 2 and spot-checked by adversary 1); Univ. of Manitoba thesis "Medications in human milk" (224 studies, 186 medications, collection and assay methods); FSANZ 2019 "Medicines or drugs of abuse in human milk and human milk products" (HMBANA donor deferral "five times the half-life of the medication"); EMA CVMP adopted milk-withdrawal guideline rev 1 (opened by adversary 3: n≥20 animals, twice-daily milkings, four-quarter composites, LOQ ≤ MRL1, 95/95 tolerance limit on per-subject Time-To-Safe-Concentration, and a 12-hour conventional fallback when most concentrations are below LOQ).
Novelty — how this differs from each: vs 1, Fomina grades evidence strength across four LactMed categories rather than against numeric depletion-study design criteria, and computes no interval — but she runs the census over the candidate's own source, own population and own drug-list concept and publishes the "how many of X" number, so what remains of limb A is a yardstick swap on an answered question. vs 2, Meer audits against FDA/ILCA rather than veterinary criteria and covers one drug class — but it is the same genre, the same faults (subject count, samples per dose interval) and the same output shape, so the record's novelty ground that "adequacy against numeric design criteria was not found" is false as written. vs 3, Damoiseaux covers 3 oncology drugs, uses prediction intervals rather than a 95/95 tolerance limit, runs no census and makes no comparison with current advice — so limb B is pre-empted in device and direction (menu of declared limits → upper-bound discard interval) but not in scope or standard; no adversary verified limb B as duplicated, and none verified it as clear either.
Novelty confidence: **Medium**, restored from the record's Low on the judge's post-Gate-5 verification (2026-10-16; independent fresh-context checker, 14 queries, 0 refusals, log in batches/2026-10-16-0833/UQ-20261016-23-verification.md), and narrowed to scope-and-standard. **Fomina et al. 2023 is not this question over the same source.** It is a presence-of-evidence census — does any study exist, in which LactMed content category, and is it a case report or a PK/cohort/RCT — and it contains no design criterion whatever: no sampling-schedule, steady-state, sample-size, collection-completeness or LOQ requirement. Reading its 51%/2% as having settled design ADEQUACY conflates "no study exists" with "the existing study's data are unfittable", which are different findings; its instrument cannot answer the candidate's question even though both run over LactMed. The fatal Disguise kill built on it is therefore withdrawn. **Meer et al. 2015 is a genuine prior and must now be cited**: it audits human lactation PK studies against a named external standard (FDA plus ILCA) and already reports the two defects a residue-depletion lens would most want to claim — insufficient samples within a dosing interval, and unreported sampling methods. So "nobody has audited published human milk PK data against an external design standard" is false and is struck from the record. What is unoccupied is the scope (Meer covers 19 anticonvulsants across 62 studies, not LactMed-wide) and the standard (nobody has applied veterinary residue-depletion requirements — VICH GL48, EMA/CVMP/SWP/735418/2012 Rev.1 — to human milk data). The stronger novelty claim of the two is limb B, tolerance-limit interruption intervals against a stated infant-exposure limit, which is genuinely unoccupied.
Grounds: downgraded from the record's Medium. The transplant vocabulary genuinely has no human-lactation hits across 40 queries, five languages and nine field jargons, but the census limb — the limb the record made stand-alone and load-bearing — was already executed and published twice in the candidate's own literature (Fomina 2023; Meer 2015), each surfaced on a single query in a vocabulary Gate 2 never tried, and a third corpus enumeration exists (Manitoba thesis). Disguise searches were executed by all three adversaries (9 each), so Disguise is verified, not unverified.
Significance — consequence: a near-zero census would convert "lactation data are poor" into a costed, regulator-legible study specification (subject count, sampling grid, terminal-phase coverage, LOQ) with an existing calculator; a qualifying subset would quantify, in regulator units, how much conservatism sits in round-hour advice, in either direction. Weakened at Gate 4: the imported guideline itself falls back to a convention in the sparse-data regime human milk data occupy ("no meaningful calculation of a 95/95 tolerance limit is possible" → "acceptable to establish a withdrawal period of 12 hours"), and the human donor-milk chain already runs a quantitative convention (5 × half-life), so the "statistics for cows, round hours for mothers" contrast is materially softer than the record's anchoring assumed.
Significance — audience: real, named and verifiably active — LactMed curators (P.O. Anderson co-authors Yeung 2023), Medications & Mothers' Milk authors, ABM/AAP committees, FDA and EMA lactation programmes, the concePTION/Milk4baby community, nuclear-medicine physicists, and anaesthesia/oncology services. Counter-evidence: the field's stated position is that "mothers are too often discouraged from starting or continuing lactation" (Monfort 2025), it has already built its own evidence-grading instrument (Fomina 2023) without asking for a veterinary design standard, and it is moving its endpoint to infant systemic exposure (UAR, PBPK), i.e. away from the units limb B reports.
Significance — fecundity: what is the human-milk analogue of an MRL and who sets it; should the endpoint be milk concentration, infant systemic exposure or an outcome; what does a 95/95 population tolerance limit mean when the consumer is a single infant with immature clearance; can a per-subject time-to-safe-concentration tolerance limit be estimated from sparse pooled literature data, and at what loss of coverage; does the audit transfer to donor-milk deferral, semen, dialysate and occupational re-entry intervals.
Significance — anchoring: the lactation evidence gap ("therapeutic orphan"), to which it offers an instrument rather than a lament; the regulatory asymmetry between dairy withdrawal intervals and human interruption advice (found stated nowhere, even in passing, across all 40 queries); model-informed drug development's extension to lactation; the nuclear-medicine/pharmacology boundary inside one hospital.
Reason for silence: nominated mechanism — a statutory-liability boundary: the veterinary calculation exists because a consumer residue limit is law and a food business is liable, nothing analogous binds human milk, and no committee, journal or reviewer pool spans the two literatures; reinforced by a directional disincentive (the field reads "how long should milk be withheld?" as adverse framing) and by recent enabling conditions (public withdrawal calculators, FDA lactation-study guidance). Status at Gate 4: accepted by adversaries 1 and 2 (the incentive limb evidenced by a quoted line from the field's own 2025 methods paper plus documented vocabulary absence), but falsified on its own test case by adversary 3 — donor human milk IS regulated as a food, FSANZ issued imported-food risk advice on medicines in human milk to a national agriculture department in 2019, the recipient is a third-party consumer of pooled pasteurised milk, and a quantitative withholding rule exists there, yet the depletion-study machinery still was not imported; the offered fallback ("milk banking is too small a niche") is unevidenced and reduces to "no one thought of it", which is not an acceptable mechanism.
Adversarial log (8 rows: attack | objection | response | status): three independent fresh-context adversaries (A1, A2, A3 — logs verbatim at batches/2026-10-16-0833/UQ-20261016-23-adversary-1.md, -2.md, -3.md; 9 new-vocabulary queries and 4 fetches each). Worst status per attack shown. **A fourth** fresh-context adversary ran afterwards at the judge's direction, because the batch's rejection rate had fallen to 40% and LEDGER.md's operating rules treat a low rate as a warning that the adversaries were too gentle. Held to the new Gate 4 standard (its own technical claims and priors cited to primary sources it opened), it returned **Provisional** — Disguise **Resolved**, every other attack Partial, no Unresolved; 10 Disguise queries in six outside vocabularies, 0 refusals. Verbatim log: batches/2026-10-16-0833/UQ-20261016-23-adversary-4.md. Its Resolved on Disguise is independent confirmation that A3's fatal Disguise kill does not stand.
1. Triviality | Limb A's sign is forecastable in a page: 714/1408 (51%) LactMed drugs have no data at all and so fail every criterion, and veterinary criteria are strictly stricter (A3, from Fomina's counts — labelled A3's own inference); 2% strong data and Milk4baby's 29/50 point the same way (A2) | The per-criterion profile inside the 47% minimal-moderate band, and which criterion fails by how much, is unreported and is what a study specification needs; no source shows the residual band is empty | Partial (A1, A3); Resolved (A2)
2. Disguise | Tested in 27 new queries across German *Wartezeit/Karenzzeit*, French, Spanish, Japanese, FARAD residue-avoidance, industrial hygiene, Codex/JECFA, historical "withhold nursing", reference-concordance, pharmacometrics, One Health, donor-milk banking, meta-research and answer-side number searches. The transplant is not renamed anywhere; but limb A is already executed work in the candidate's own field — Meer 2015 audits 62 lactation studies over 19 drugs against an externally published design standard, faulting participant numbers and samples per dose interval; Fomina 2023 runs the census over LactMed and "commonly administered medications in lactating women" and publishes the number Gate 2 declared unobtainable; the Manitoba thesis enumerates 224 studies / 186 medications; FSANZ 2019 records a 5 × half-life human withholding rule, falsifying the claim that the coinage is absent from human pharmacotherapy outside radiopharmaceuticals | The conjunction was still not found: no paper imports numeric veterinary criteria, computes an interval, or compares computed intervals with current advice | **Unresolved (A3)**; Resolved-with-downgrade (A1), Partial (A2)
3. Combinatorial novelty | Veterinary × lactation with the interface problem parked in presupposition 2 and relocated to Fecundity; strip the costume and the human side already issues design guidance | Fails: the seam is specific and sharpened by the guideline — the harmonised statistic is a tolerance limit over per-subject times-to-safe-concentration, requiring every subject followed below the limit, a structure pooled opportunistic human data lacks; no human-side decision rule exists (Monfort names RID with no cutoff; Damoiseaux invented limits "for demonstration purposes") | Resolved (A3); Partial (A1, A2)
4. Presupposition failure | The record's firewall contradicts the guideline it imports: the question's own criteria "assay LOQ relative to the limit" and "terminal-phase coverage" are defined by the guideline relative to the MRL ("provided that the LOQ is sufficiently below or equal to the MRL1"; "if the last concentration in the data set is still above MRL1, TTSCi cannot be calculated"), so adequacy cannot be scored until the ceiling is fixed — the claim that "the census limb (A) does not depend on it", and the 3/3 well-posedness rationale resting on it, are false (A3, quoting the opened EMA guideline). Separately, the veterinary rule bounds a concentration while every candidate human limit is a dose, so volume/fat/bioavailability must enter (A2, unsourced); and presupposition 4 is contested by three groups, not one | Repairable by reporting limb A as a matrix over the pre-stated ceiling set — but the repair concedes that no ceiling-independent limb exists, which was the feature keeping the question answerable while the field's central dispute is open | **Unresolved (A3)**; Partial (A1, A2)
5. Vagueness | Pass rates are tunable by criterion choice; "each design criterion a veterinary regulator imposes" is not one fixed set (EMA milk vs tissue vs US routes), the rule is given as "e.g. 95/95", and the drug list has no canonical derivation | Criteria fixed in advance from a named guideline (n≥20, 12-h milkings, four-quarter composites, LOQ-vs-limit, 95/95 TTSC, all read off the adopted text), pre-registration, per-criterion reporting, signed hours with zero for "no interruption"; limb A returns a definite number including zero | Resolved (A2, A3); Partial (A1 — the question does not name which veterinary route supplies the rule, and that choice moves limb B's numbers)
6. Significance inflation | The audience has a standing directional commitment this cuts against and is migrating to infant-systemic-exposure metrics; oncology already gets discard intervals drug by drug; and the asymmetry is weaker than claimed — the imported guideline itself falls back to a 12-hour convention when most concentrations are below LOQ, and donor milk already runs 5 × half-life, so thin data gets a convention on both sides of the species line | Audience existence and current activity are evidenced (Yeung 2023: 28 providers interviewed on this decision, LactMed's editor a co-author); the census output is actionable whichever way it lands | Partial (A1, A2, A3)
7. Reason for silence | Liability explains why the data were never mandated, not why nobody asked; and the mechanism fails its own test case — donor human milk is regulated as a food with a third-party consumer and a quantitative withholding rule (FSANZ 2019), and the machinery still was not imported; half the bridge is already built from the far side (EMA CVMP on children's milk intake) | A1/A2: the incentive/taboo limb does the work, evidenced by the field's own stated position plus a vocabulary absence across five languages. A3: the "niche too small" fallback is unevidenced and reduces to "no one thought of it" | Unresolved (A3); Resolved (A1, A2)
8. Dissolution | With no MRL analogue the interval is a function of a limit the investigator picks, so the output is a calculator and the comparison sets one convention beside another | Fails: limb A terminates in a per-criterion table and cannot dissolve; a sensitivity surface over declared limits is an accepted result form in this field (Damoiseaux 2023 published exactly that shape); conditional is not dissolved | Resolved (A1, A2, A3)
Scores: Well-posedness 2/3 · Significance 2/3
Well-posedness reduced from the record's 3/3: both limbs still state what would settle them, but the ceiling-independence of limb A — the explicit basis for 3/3 — is contradicted by the imported guideline's own LOQ-vs-MRL and terminal-phase definitions, so the contested central presupposition is not neutralised, only deferred. Significance held at 2/3, and weakened further by the guideline's own sparse-data convention and the existing donor-milk convention.
Strongest remaining objection: **Limb B's qualifying subset is near-certainly empty before the first extraction, and limb A then has to carry the question alone.** The one criterion in the imported standard that is both numeric and independent of any infant-exposure limit is the sample-size floor — "Data should be available for a representative sample of n animals, with n>=20", and "a sample size n = 20 is the very minimum" — and the human corpus fails it by construction: FDA's lactation guidance sets no sample size, and the best registered milk-only studies plan 8 to 16 women, with sample sizes declared not to rest on "empirical or hypothesis testing criteria". For the datasets that do exist, the tolerance-limit rule is then inapplicable by its own stated condition, since time-to-safe-concentration cannot be calculated when the last measured concentration is still above the limit. That leaves limb A, whose headline is already in print in adjacent grading (Fomina 2023: 2% of 1,408 LactMed drugs "strong"), and whose advertised payoff — a regulator-legible specification for the study that would fix the gap — is a transcription of the EMA guideline's own numbers and needs no census at all. The genuinely new and genuinely unforeseeable residue is narrow: **which criterion binds for which drug**, a distinction real datasets do vary on.
Secondary, and corrected rather than fatal: the record's claim that limb A is independent of the infant-exposure limit is false for two of its five criteria — the LOQ criterion is stated only as "provided that the LOQ is sufficiently below or equal to the MRL1", with "sufficiently" never defined, and terminal-phase adequacy is not a sample count or a half-life multiple but a limit-relative applicability test. The repair is licensed by the source document rather than invented: footnote 1 states "In the absence of a numerical MRL, another reference value may be used as the relevant limit for residue concentrations", and §4.1.1 adds that for substances without an MRL the relevant safe concentration "might be based on an ADI or other scientifically justified health based guidance value". So limb A becomes a small surface scored once per candidate limit rather than a scalar — an assumption to declare in the design, not a reason to kill the study.
Provisional at: Gate 5. No attack stands Unresolved — A3's fatal Disguise and presupposition kills were both downgraded on verification (Fomina is not a duplicate; the limit-dependence is repairable under the guideline's own footnote 1), and a fourth adversary at the strict standard Resolved Disguise outright and left every other attack Partial. Well-posedness 2/3 caps it at Provisional independently. **What would promote it:** re-scope onto the residue that survives — which criterion binds for which drug — and in the process (i) strike the claim that limb A is independent of the exposure limit and pre-state a set of candidate reference values, scoring the two limit-relative criteria once per limit; (ii) pre-register numeric values for the two criteria the source guideline leaves as the undefined word "sufficiently"; (iii) add individual-participant-data availability and an explicit cross-study pooling rule to the criterion list, since the n>=20 floor is otherwise failed by construction and limb B has no corpus; and (iv) cite Meer et al. 2015 and Fomina et al. 2023 as prior art rather than as absent. With those, well-posedness reaches 3/3 and the Validated bar is in reach on the present novelty finding. Suggested first step toward an answer (pointer only — do not take it): before any extraction, count how many published human milk datasets reach n>=20 at all. If the answer is near zero, as the registered-study sample sizes suggest, limb B has no corpus and the question is the criterion-binding census alone.
Routing (if rejected as already-asked): Not applicable — not rejected, and nothing is routed. The design-adequacy question is partly occupied rather than open (Meer et al. 2015 audits lactation PK studies against FDA plus ILCA), which the operating rules exclude from routing, and the interruption-interval limb was not found posed anywhere, so it is not an asked-but-open problem either.

ID: UQ-20261016-24
Date: 2026-10-16
Status: Provisional
Domain(s): STEM — quantum computing (cloud-accessible superconducting/trapped-ion processors); metascience of hardware benchmarking; measurement/metrology of reported results

Question (canonical): For a pre-specified corpus of papers reporting results executed on named cloud-accessible quantum processors, and a pre-specified per-device figure of merit F built from archived calibration fields and stable across a declared comparability window (same hardware revision, same recalibration methodology): (a) what fraction of published results can be located in time to the archive's granularity, and what fraction of those fall inside a window the archive still covers; and (b) among the locatable-and-covered results, is the percentile rank of F at the reported execution window — within a pre-specified symmetric comparison window (e.g. ±30 days, truncated at revision boundaries) — uniform on [0,1] or shifted towards favourable ranks, and by how much, reported both as a shift in expected device quality and, on a pre-declared monotone subset of result types, as the implied shift in the headline number? (Gate 1 reformulation, the single permitted one; the as-intaken version is in the record.)

Alternative formulations:
- Do quantum-computing papers report runs made when the machine happened to be good, and can that selection be measured from the vendor's own calibration history?
- What is the percentile rank, within a device's own recent calibration record, of the device state behind each published result obtained on it?

Motivating gap: New-instrument candidate. Vendors publish per-qubit calibration data (T1, T2, gate and readout errors) nominally retrievable for past dates, while papers name the backend and often a date; drift over hours to days is well characterised (arXiv:2105.09472; arXiv:2208.07219; IEEE DataPort temporal-error study; caslab.io/publications/xu2023long.pdf), and error-aware layout / just-in-time transpilation (arXiv:2606.27508; arXiv:2005.12820; Cirq "Qubit Picking") exist to exploit the current calibration state — sensible practice that is also a selection mechanism on the published record. Gate 2 found the normative half already stated in-field (arXiv:2411.08860, Principle 4: "from which best results are selected post hoc") and Gate 4 found the sensitivity half quantified in-field (arXiv:2605.29872: the same ZNE configuration's effect size >3x larger "depending solely on when it is executed"), but no archive-to-literature join and no selection estimand. The gap is narrower than intaken: the worry and the mechanism are on record; the quantity is not.

Presuppositions:
- P1 (CONTESTED, load-bearing, now evidenced as failing in part): historical calibration data are retrievable for the periods the published results fall in. Gate 4 evidence: IBM documents `backend.properties(datetime=...)` ("timestamp closest to, but older than, the specified datetime") and CSV calibration download, with no retention depth stated anywhere; the current API reference raises `NotImplementedError` "If datetime is specified when IBM Quantum Compute is used"; `IBMRetiredBackend.properties()` is stubbed to return `None` (Qiskit/qiskit-ibm-runtime issue #2255, open since 2025-05-08, no maintainer reply; earlier #1069, #1127 record `datetime` unsupported on the cloud channel in 2023). Third-party mirrors are sporadic snapshots (GitHub repo search: 0 systematic mirrors; `fake_provider` one-off `props_<device>.json` files dominate); the one mirror opened covers "90 days" on four unnamed IBM machines (Zenodo 4898393).
- P2 (CONTESTED): papers report enough detail to locate a run in time. The locatable fraction is itself a reportable quantity. arXiv:2607.08348 (127 manual + ~5,000 automated papers) carries a "hardware description" indicator but, in fetched text from two independent adversaries, reports no backend-named / date-given / calibration-snapshot fraction — the number is genuinely not in hand. Supporting: many hardware papers do print a run-time calibration table for the qubits used (A1/S2), so the fraction is plausibly non-trivial.
- P3 (CONTESTED): a time-comparable F can be built from the archived fields; recalibration methodology, qubit retirement and revisions change what fields mean, so comparability windows must be pre-specified and truncated at revision boundaries.
- P4: the null is well defined — absent selection, run-time ranks are uniform. Holds by construction only if (i) the window is fixed before any rank is computed, (ii) calendar time is exchangeable within it, and (iii) F is not selected on the run day's own snapshot. Adversary 3 raised (iii) as an unflagged defect: F as written (median two-qubit error over the qubits actually used) is biased towards favourable ranks under the null, because those qubits were picked on the run-day snapshot and a quantity selected on a noisy estimate regresses to the mean on other days. Status per the adversary's own labelling: its own unsourced reasoning, scoped to snapshot-selected subsets, vanishing for a device-level aggregate or a pre-fixed subset — so Partial, not fatal, and a fallback F removes it.
- P5: headline numbers depend monotonically on F for at least a subset of result types (supported for one class by Senapati et al., IEEE QCE 2023, on their own runs). The monotone subset is still undeclared on any named result class.
- P6 (NOT presupposed, stated to block a misreading): that any selection is misconduct or that re-runs were concealed.

What would count as an answer: A pre-registered pipeline over a named paper sample and named backends reporting, per result, the percentile rank of F at the reported run window within the pre-specified comparison window; test is uniformity of those ranks (KS or one-sided mean-rank with a pre-stated effect size), reported as a shift in expected device quality and, on the declared monotone subset, as the implied shift in the headline number. "Ranks uniform" is a full answer (though attenuated: it bounds the effect within the date-reporting subset, measured through a daily-snapshot proxy, rather than retiring the concern). The locatable-and-covered fraction is part of the answer. A demonstration that archive retention does not reach the literature is a feasibility verdict, not an answer.

Novelty — queries run (query → one-line result): 38 distinct documented queries — 13 at Gate 2 (own-field own-words title query; mandatory fraction-limb query; lay, drift/stability, metrology/SPC, astronomy observing-conditions, clinical/metascience selective-reporting, benchmark-standardisation vocabularies) and 25 Disguise queries across three independent adversaries (A1: clinical-lab QC, HPC/SPEC run rules, semiconductor-fab tool health, German, paper-reported snapshot tables, metascience forking-paths, "reported vs typical"; A2: photovoltaic "hero data/champion device", proteomics repository a-posteriori QC, finance sample-period selection, Millikan-era HPS apparatus-condition selection, HEP good-run lists, Chinese-language quantum, agronomy site-years, in-field "hero run" slang, generic instrument-log-to-publication join; A3: Pelofske vendor-vs-user QV, cloud job/machine characterisation, Hoefler & Belli HPC reporting, reported-snapshot meta-analysis, reserved-vs-open-queue tuning, German, Metriq/QED-C benchmark tracking, winner's-curse/regression-to-the-mean qubit selection). Most informative: "cherry-picking favourable calibration quantum computer experiments reporting bias best day" → arXiv:2411.08860 (names post-hoc best-result selection, measures nothing); "what fraction of quantum computing papers report backend name and run date calibration metadata survey reproducibility" → arXiv:2607.08348 (fraction not published); A2/q2 proteomics a-posteriori QC → scores deposited runs for reuse, inverting the move; A2/q9 and A3/D4 (answer-side, generic and in-field) → no instrument-log-to-publication join found in any field; A3/P1 + GitHub issue search → the retention evidence above. 17 sources opened (5 record fetches, 12 adversary fetches) plus free GitHub code/issue search; one arXiv export-API call refused (robots/proxy) and recorded. Full lists: batches/2026-10-16-0833/UQ-20261016-24-record.md and UQ-20261016-24-adversary-1/-2/-3.md.

Novelty — nearest prior formulations (3, with sources):
1. arXiv:2605.29872, Köster & Mauerer, "Claim against Measurement: Statistical Artefacts in Quantum Error Mitigation Benchmarks" (v2, 24 Jul 2026) — opened independently by all three adversaries. 81 QEM papers reviewed; 132-configuration ZNE sweep with "hardware calibration ... not merely incidental but active"; 72-hour hardware study, effect size >3x larger "depending solely on when it is executed"; proposes minimum reporting standards including longitudinal drift assessment.
2. arXiv:2411.08860, "How NOT to Fool the Masses When Giving Performance Results for Quantum Computers" (2024) — Principle 4 names post-hoc selection of best results as cherry-picking; recommends disclosure of test designs and tuning policies. Normative ancestor: Hoefler & Belli, SC15 (confirmed real, A3/D3).
3. arXiv:2609.27704, Larrucea, "The winner's curse in hardware VQE" (v2, 1 Oct 2026) — closest existing measurement of selection bias in publication-grade hardware results: non-retained fraction 0.989 ([0.906, 1.072]) on re-measurement, two IBM Heron r3 processors, drift acknowledged as a competing explanation.
Also adjacent, opened: arXiv:2607.08348 ("Works on My QPU": 24.4%/26.8% code availability, 64.5% execution failure; no backend/date fraction); arXiv:2203.03816 (Pelofske et al., user-measured QV "typically lag[s] behind officially reported results", no timing attribution, no archive); Senapati et al., IEEE QCE 2023. Residual unopened neighbours: arXiv:2203.13121 (cloud job/machine characteristics), arXiv:2508.21231 (qubit-health analytics), arXiv:2603.08680.

Novelty — how this differs from each:
- vs 2605.29872: establishes prospectively, on its own runs, that execution epoch moves a published-grade conclusion, and prescribes drift reporting. No archive join, no publication-corpus run dates, no rank/percentile estimand, no selection measurement. It is the strongest narrowing of this candidate: the mechanism and the reform are both in print in-field from one group; only the retrospective measurement of selection on the record is absent.
- vs 2411.08860: asserts the practice and prescribes disclosure; defines no estimand, uses no archive. The candidate converts an in-field accusation into a pre-registered falsifiable quantity with an exact null and archive-based rather than self-reported evidence.
- vs 2609.27704: same family, different selection channel (finite-shot/optimizer winner's curse inside one campaign) and different evidence (prospective re-measurement, with drift as a confounder to difference away). The candidate makes drift the selection variable, acts at the level of the published record, and is retrospective, needing no device time and covering non-participating authors.
- vs 2607.08348 / 2203.03816: artefact-side reproducibility indicators and vendor-claim-vs-user-achievable benchmarks respectively; neither recovers the device's physical state at run time, which is this candidate's whole object.

Novelty confidence: Medium (thin). Nothing in 38 vocabularies, and nothing in 17 opened sources, joins a vendor calibration archive to published run dates or tests uniformity of run-time state percentiles; all three adversaries resolved Disguise. Not High: the normative half (2411.08860) and the timing-as-artefact half with reporting standards attached (2605.29872) are both on record in the candidate's own field in 2026, a close empirical neighbour exists (2609.27704), and the structural move belongs to a mature facility-records-to-publications tradition. Not Low: no near-duplicate; the specific measurable appeared nowhere.

Significance — consequence: If ranks shift high, the output is a quantified correction factor on the published NISQ record with a cheap attached reform (report run timestamp plus contemporaneous calibration snapshot), and an archive-based account of poor cross-group replication that currently rests on assertion plus one campaign's re-measurement. If uniform, a live in-field accusation is bounded with data and the reproducibility effort is redirected to the artefact-side failures already measured. Either way the locatability-and-coverage fraction bounds what any retrospective audit of this literature can establish.

Significance — audience: Benchmarking standard-setters (QED-C/Metriq, arXiv:2303.02108) and the IEEE QCE reproducibility track, where a timestamp-plus-snapshot checklist field costs one API call; vendors, who set the retention policy P1 depends on; referees and editors, who presently cannot ask "was this a good week for that machine?"; the 2605.29872/2607.08348 group, actively writing reporting standards about execution timing now. Deduction retained: demonstrated responsiveness is weak (this ledger's own verification at UQ-20261016-19 found the closest precedents — 26% of approved animals unreported, 47% non-publishing ESO programmes — produced no reporting-rule change), and the reform is already motivated by the drift studies alone, so this measurement is not its gating input.

Significance — fecundity: (a) the same test on error-mitigation and advantage claims, where state sensitivity is largest and 2605.29872 already shows a >3x timing swing; (b) reserved/dedicated versus open-queue rank contrast, separating one operator-side channel from author-side selection without touching intent; (c) whether rank shift predicts cross-group replication failure; (d) vendor pre-demonstration tuning as a calendar effect around announcement dates; (e) transplant of the state-percentile-at-publication statistic to GPU-cluster benchmarks, beam quality, observing conditions and clinical-assay instrument state — none of which, per the metrology, astronomy, HPC, proteomics, agronomy and photovoltaic sweeps, computes it.

Significance — anchoring: NISQ reproducibility as documented (2607.08348; Senapati et al.); the drift-characterisation corpus (2105.09472; 2208.07219; IEEE DataPort; the long-term IBM calibration study), which supplies the data and stops at the device; quantum-advantage replication disputes where "which run, when" is the crux; benchmark standardisation and vendor control-plane openness (2605.15233), which decide whether the metadata exists; the winner's-curse result (2609.27704), which would gain a publication-level counterpart.

Supporting: the conceptual turn from drift-as-device-property to drift-as-artefact-in-published-claims is dated 2026, so this is the next step of a bridge months old. Note the cost of the surviving mechanism: it is infeasibility, which this ledger classifies as grounds for routing rather than as novelty — see strongest remaining objection.

Scores: Well-posedness 2/3 · Significance 2/3

Strongest remaining objection: **Most of the literature the question is about ran on devices whose calibration history is now unreachable.** Corrected on the judge's post-Gate-5 verification (2026-10-16, independent fresh-context technical check, 22 queries, 0 refusals), because the record's version of this objection was wrong in its first clause. By-date retrieval IS implemented for currently-live IBM QPUs on the qiskit-ibm-runtime channel: `backend.properties(datetime=...)` maps to the REST parameter `updated_before`, is documented under "Retrieve historical data" in IBM's QPU-information guide, and is exercised by a live CI integration test as of release 0.50.0 (2026-09-24). The record's claim that it raises `NotImplementedError` on the current channel is withdrawn. Two real limits remain, and they carry the objection. (a) For **retired** devices there is no path at all: `IBMRetiredBackend.properties()` is a stub returning None, open issue #2255 (filed 2025-05-08) asks for exactly this capability and is still open, and IBM's retired-QPU guide offers only job retrieval — no bulk download, no published archive; the `fake_provider` snapshots cannot substitute because they carry no date. Since most published IBM hardware results ran on devices now retired, the corpus that motivates the question is largely out of reach. (b) The retained history depth is nowhere documented, no public REST reference lists `updated_before`, and the only CI coverage uses `datetime=today`, so the usable window is unverified — and that single number decides whether the live-device half of the study is viable at all. Two further corrections for a successor's design: IonQ **does** expose dated per-characterization history by REST, so any framing in which no vendor publishes dated calibration history would be wrong; and AWS Braket is the clearest negative, stating outright that historic calibration data is unavailable for all its devices. Well-posedness stays at 2/3 on this corrected basis: the question is answerable in principle and for live devices, and largely unanswerable for the literature it is about.
Promotion requires: (i) a documented by-date retrieval path — live-device history depth on the current IBM Quantum Platform plus at least one other vendor, or a named mirror (Zenodo 4898393, IEEE DataPort, caslab) — whose device/date coverage is shown to intersect a named paper corpus, with the locatable-and-covered fraction reported first (this is what would lift well-posedness to 3/3); (ii) the primary F replaced by a selection-blind construction (device-level aggregate or pre-fixed qubit subset) so the null is exact for the headline estimand, and F shown comparable across at least one documented recalibration-methodology change; (iii) a named result class with a pre-declared monotone F-to-headline mapping, plus the reserved-versus-open-queue contrast carried in the same pipeline so the composite is partly decomposed (this is what would lift significance to 3/3). Novelty is also a standing ceiling: with 2605.29872 and 2411.08860 in-field, Medium is the best available and re-verification is due if either group publishes the archive join itself.

Suggested first step toward an answer (pointer only — do not take it): settle the retention window before anything else — an audit, not a study. With credentials on IBM's current channel, measure empirically how far back `backend.properties(datetime=...)` actually returns data for two live QPUs, and record it; that one number decides whether the live-device arm exists. In parallel, document what IonQ's dated per-characterization REST history covers and over what period, since it is the one vendor archive known to be addressable by date, and record AWS Braket's stated unavailability as the negative control. Only if a usable window exists does the join to published run dates become worth specifying.

Routing (if rejected as already-asked): n/a — not rejected.

ID: UQ-20261016-25
Date: 2026-10-16
Status: Rejected
Domain(s): Medicine — clinical pharmacology, pharmacoepidemiology, drug regulation (adjacent: oncology pharmacy, health economics)
Question (canonical): Because a molecule's marketed tablet strengths define a lattice of achievable daily doses, what fraction of population-level variation in prescribed dose is imposed by that lattice rather than by patient characteristics, and when an individual strength is discontinued, does the resulting shift in the dose distribution produce measurable changes in clinical outcomes or adverse events?
Alternative formulations:
- Is the dose a patient takes chosen by the prescriber or by the manufacturer's catalogue of strengths, and what happens when the catalogue changes?
- Treating strength discontinuations as natural experiments on dose, how much do a drug's available strengths matter to outcomes?
- Is the marketed strength ladder a clinically consequential design object, or slack that prescribing absorbs without outcome cost?
- Gate 1 reformulation (permitted, both versions retained): with the achievable lattice defined empirically from dispensing data (scored halves, multi-tablet regimens at >=1%) and an unconstrained target dose from a pre-registered drug-specific target-dose model — (a) what share of the variance of dispensed daily dose is attributable to rounding onto the lattice, and what share of patients have no reachable lattice point in their target interval; (b) for strength discontinuations passing an exogeneity screen, what is the ITS/DiD effect on the dose distribution and on pre-registered clinical and adverse-event endpoints against a pre-set equivalence margin.
Motivating gap: Silence mapping — dosing guidance is dense on *how* to dose and apparently silent on why the choosable strengths are what they are; strength-level marketing-status registers looked like an unused natural experiment on dose. Gate 2 finding: **the gap does not hold.** The question was published in the candidate's own field in 1996, and strength-removal-as-exposure has been executed twice since (Ontario, 2018 and 2019).
Presuppositions: (1) dispensed daily doses and dated strength-level marketing histories retrievable at scale — contested as to completeness; (2) LOAD-BEARING: strength discontinuations are frequent and exogenous enough to instrument dose — contested, and Gate 2 worsens it: the two executed examples are payer delistings chosen *because* high doses were thought harmful, so the real supply of events is enriched for the exact endogeneity the design must exclude; (3) prescribers round rather than split/combine — partly relaxed by the empirical lattice, still contested; (4) non-flat exposure-response over the perturbed range; (5) endpoints ascertainable in the same data; (6) NEW and load-bearing: a per-patient unconstrained target dose is well defined — for titrate-to-response drugs the guideline target is an interval or not computable, so limb (a) is identified only relative to a chosen model. Not presupposed: that the lattice is badly chosen, or that regulators should mandate strengths.
What would count as an answer: (i) a pre-registered variance decomposition of dispensed daily dose into lattice-rounding and target-dose components for a stated drug set, with sensitivity across target-dose models, plus the share of patients whose target is unreachable on the empirical lattice; (ii) for exogeneity-screened strength discontinuations, ITS/DiD estimates on the dose distribution and on pre-registered clinical/adverse-event endpoints against an equivalence margin fixed in advance. A heaping plot is a premise, not an answer.
Novelty — queries run (query → one-line result): 12 web searches (cap was 11 — overrun recorded, not hidden) plus 6 WebFetch attempts of which 1 returned readable content; full list in batches/2026-10-16-0833/UQ-20261016-25-record.md. Most informative: (8) "levothyroxine prescribed dose distribution peaks at commercially available strengths rounding pharmacy claims" → **decisive**: index record for "EFFECTS OF RESTRICTING LEVOTHYROXINE DOSAGE STRENGTH AVAILABILITY"; (10) extended Ain-1996 query → PMID 8947984, DOI 10.1002/j.1875-9114.1996.tb03039.x confirmed on two further independent hosts; (11) "withdrawal of a drug strength forced dose change interrupted time series dose distribution national prescribing data" → **decisive**: Ontario high-strength opioid delisting ITS (PMC6518867); (12) extended → Martins 2019 (DOI 10.1002/pds.4764) plus a second strength-delisting study (PMID 29911823); (7) "percentage of patients whose calculated dose cannot be achieved with commercially available tablet strengths" → no published fraction found for any drug, class or dataset (the one limb not found already computed); (6) bunching/kink-notch vocabulary (economics) → bunching econometrics only, never applied to dose strengths; (5) dose banding / dose rounding (oncology pharmacy) → ISOPP 2017, NHS England SACT: the vial-size lattice is openly discussed as a lattice, for injectables. Retrieval failures recorded: Europe PMC 429, Wiley and PubMed fetch errors, PMC reCAPTCHA, two curl attempts blocked by the proxy (CONNECT 403) — consequence: Ain 1996 verified at title/author/journal/year/volume/page/PMID/DOI level, abstract never read, so its design, endpoints and conclusion are not asserted.
Novelty — nearest prior formulations (3, with sources):
P1. Ain KB et al., "Effects of restricting levothyroxine dosage strength availability", *Pharmacotherapy* 1996;16(6):1103-1110. PMID 8947984; DOI 10.1002/j.1875-9114.1996.tb03039.x (index record opened: acnpsearch.tweb-dev.unibo.it/singlejournalindex/273195).
P2. Martins D et al., "Impact of delisting high-strength opioid formulations from a public drug benefit formulary on opioid utilization in Ontario, Canada", *Pharmacoepidemiol Drug Saf* 2019. DOI 10.1002/pds.4764; PMC6518867.
P3. "Evaluating the early impacts of delisting high-strength opioids on patterns of prescribing in Ontario" (2018), PMID 29911823 — title and PMID from search results, not opened.
Adjacent, not counted: ISOPP Dose Rounding Position Paper 2017; NHS England SACT dose banding; a Dutch forced dose-equivalent levothyroxine brand-switch/TSH cohort (Nivel, Flinterman).
Novelty — how this differs from each: vs P1 — limb (b) *is* this paper's title; the differences are scope and method (multi-drug, manufacturer rather than formulary removals, exogeneity screen, equivalence margin), not question, and even that rests on a design never read. vs P2 — identical design logic on opioids; the candidate adds instrument framing, clinical/adverse-event endpoints and pre-registration, i.e. endpoint extension and design hardening of an executed study. vs P3 — same event, earlier window; establishes that strength removal shifts the dose distribution, which the candidate concedes is a premise. Surviving residue: limb (a) only — no published variance decomposition and no published unreachable-target fraction found (query 7).
Novelty confidence: Low for limb (b); limb (a) is unoccupied but was never posed — split on the judge's post-Gate-5 verification (2026-10-16, independent fresh-context sweep, 23 queries, of which 9 failed on access rather than on content: PubMed, PMC, Wiley, Semantic Scholar and the Europe PMC API returned reCAPTCHA, HTTP 429 or client errors, so no MeSH or field-restricted bibliographic search was possible). Limb (b) is answered, with three qualifications the record got wrong: Ain et al. 1996 is real and its title is essentially as reported, and it is a randomised trial that measured patient outcomes (thyroid function tests) under a restricted strength formulary and found no significant change — but it restricted a **set** of strengths rather than discontinuing one; the Ontario delistings removed **five products at once** and measured dispensing and dose trajectories, not clinical outcomes, with Guan et al. themselves calling for patient-level outcome work. So limb (b) is answered for levothyroxine in a specialist randomised trial and remains unanswered for opioids at the clinical-outcome level. Limb (a), the variance share attributable to the strength lattice, has not been computed in any drug class — but it has also never been **posed**: it appears nowhere as a question, a parameter to estimate, or a stated research gap. The phenomenon is named in print (the 3D-printing and scored-tablet literature says required strengths "may not be available") and its coarser version is both posed and descriptively answered — Zhang 2021 reports 22% of prescriptions not fillable on the marketed lattice. Limb (a) is therefore a novel **framing** of a known, partly quantified phenomenon, which is neither a disguised known nor an open question in the literature. Treat the absence as not-found rather than established, given the access failures above.
Significance — consequence: both branches decision-relevant (ladder density as an approval/listing condition, or a bounded null that positively justifies manufacturer discretion), but discounted: P1-P3 already establish the existence of a dose shift, so only magnitudes are at stake.
Significance — audience: real and standing — FDA CDER marketing-status/shortage staff and EMA Article 57 holders, P&T and formulary committees (who make exactly the P2/P3 decision), generic manufacturers choosing strengths, guideline writers, paediatric/renal dosing specialists. Not inflated; but P2/P3 show the audience already acts here, which is also evidence the question is not new to them.
Significance — fecundity: strength-ladder design as a granularity/lot-sizing problem; whether a scored tablet substitutes for a strength; minimum ladder density for narrow-therapeutic-index drugs; interaction with weight- and eGFR-band dosing; paediatric incentives framed as ladder density.
Significance — anchoring: drug-shortage epidemiology, oncology dose banding/rounding, pill-splitting safety, strength-specific NTI bioequivalence policy (EMA levothyroxine guidance), paediatric age-appropriate formulations.
Reason for silence: proposed mechanism was a disciplinary boundary plus an unowned object (the ladder is set commercially; clinical pharmacology owns exposure-response, health economics price, regulatory science per-strength bioequivalence), secondarily data recency. Gate 2 undercuts the premise: there was no silence, only a thin, drug-specific, lightly cited literature — consistent with the Low novelty finding.

Strongest remaining objection: The candidate bundles an answered limb with a reframing. Limb (b) is essentially the title of Ain et al. 1996 in its own field and the strength-removal natural experiment has been run twice since in Ontario, so nothing of it is un-asked; limb (a) is unoccupied but was never posed by anyone, and its coarser form is already answered descriptively (Zhang 2021: 22% of prescriptions not fillable on the marketed lattice), so it is a variance-decomposition restatement of a documented phenomenon rather than a new object of inquiry. A ledger entry needs a question that was not asked; this is one question that was asked and answered next to one that nobody asked because the phenomenon was already visible.
Suggested first step toward an answer (pointer only — do not take it): Not pursued. If limb (a) is ever revisited it needs an indexed bibliographic search first (MeSH or field-restricted), which this run could not perform — PubMed, PMC, Wiley, Semantic Scholar and the Europe PMC API were all unreachable — because a null on a variance-decomposition phrasing is exactly the kind of result a proper indexed search overturns. It would then need a defensible target-dose model, since the variance share is identified only relative to one, and Zhang 2021's 22% unfillable fraction as its benchmark.
Routing (if rejected as already-asked): **Not routed**, and the row the batch proposed for limb (a) is deliberately dropped. Limb (b) is answered (Ain 1996; the two Ontario delisting studies), and answered rejections are excluded by the operating rules. Limb (a) is not asked-but-open either: an independent check found it posed nowhere in print — not as a question, not as a parameter, not as a stated gap — so routing it would hand the research workstream a question this ledger invented and then rejected, under the label of an open problem. The honest classification is "novel framing of a known phenomenon", which belongs in neither file; it is recorded in the batch report instead.
